evidence.clarity: “Every truck gets a door and a time” is immediately explained as carriers booking a dock window instead of calling receiving or waiting in the yard.
evidence.fit: The warehouse manager sees the sample/pilot caveat and a 30-minute demo link; the carrier sees a separate booking link.
evidence.distinctiveness: The dock drawing and time-by-door board show the exact warehouse and dispatch workflow rather than stock fleet imagery.
evidence.proof: At 390 I used the clock and selected Door 3; open slot 08:00 showed a carrier/reference/trailer form, and the done state supplied a gate reference and late-arrival rule.
evidence.craft: The one-door mobile list stays legible and the headline/action are clear; the probe reports no overflow at 320/390/768/1440.
evidence.mobile: 390: as a dispatcher I can switch among doors and scroll down their open hours without sideways table movement; the warehouse demo CTA remains above the fold.
evidence.honesty: The copy says the two pilot warehouses cannot be named and results are not measured, while the booking form states it is a local sample and sends nothing.
evidence.interaction: At 1440/768/390, each of six door tabs changes the displayed slots; clock limits update the sample, empty carrier is rejected, and a valid booking can be reset.
evidence.copy: “Your warehouse’s booking page” separates the carrier journey from the manager’s demo, and the empty-carrier error tells the user why it is required.
evidence.first_screen: 1440 shows the dock wall and beginning of the grid beside the promise; at 390 the drawing and clock are visible, with the booking row list one scroll below.

problems: The sample booking only changes local state and does not reserve a live appointment.
The menu does not close on Escape, so keyboard users must press Menu again or follow a link.
The mobile first screen shows the dock face rather than the open appointment grid.

evidence.clarity: The hero says Dockline publishes dock slots and that carriers book a time instead of calling or queuing; both audiences have a named link.
evidence.fit: The warehouse manager sees the demo URL; a dispatcher gets a distinct booking URL and the sample-board limitation is visible.
evidence.distinctiveness: The large industrial board and before/after dock timeline make the operational job easy to picture.
evidence.proof: Choosing an open board cell opens a dispatcher form; a valid PO produces a local reference and gate instructions, with “sample data” visible nearby.
evidence.craft: The page is visually coherent, but the probe reports 11px text and 44 elements under 12px; board labels are dense in the dark schedule.
evidence.mobile: At 390 the board shows only early columns and later booking windows require sideways scroll; the repeated small slot details are hard to read on a phone.
evidence.honesty: The board is labeled sample/made-up carriers and the pilots/results statement matches the brief.
evidence.interaction: At 390 I selected all open-window controls, submitted no PO to see an inline error, tried zero/negative/long values, and used Book another; the board itself is horizontally scrollable.
evidence.copy: The 15-minute early/20-minute late grace rule and PO/BOL language are useful to dispatchers; the warehouse conversion action has a specific 30-minute demo destination.
evidence.first_screen: 1440: the promise and board occupy the first screen. At 390 the first columns show, but most usable booking windows and their controls lie offscreen to the right.

problems: The mobile schedule requires sideways scrolling and reduces core appointment details to 11px, so it is not usable for a dispatcher reading on a phone.
The artifact dominates the page before a mobile user can reach the booking form, and the layout gives no menu control at phone size.
Zero and negative pallet counts are blocked by native constraints, but the booking reference accepts zero/negative text and long PO values without bounds.

hard_fail_flags.evidence: At 390 the core booking board is a horizontally scrollable 22-column schedule; only early times fit in the visible strip, later booking buttons require sideways scrolling, and the probe finds 44 text elements below 12px (11px minimum) in the repeated slot details.
hard_fail_flags.steps: Open B/index.html at 390×844 and inspect the board. The initial view shows 06:00–08:00 while the schedule continues to 17:00; scroll `.board-scroll` horizontally to expose later times and booking buttons. The probe reports 44 elements under 12px.

reason: As the warehouse manager, I can see the sample limits and book a demo; as the dispatcher, the door tabs and vertical open-hour list are easier to use on a phone than B’s sideways board. B has a strong, concrete operational story, but I would reconsider if the board reflowed to a readable mobile view.
